title: Containers and Kubernetes: namespaces, cgroups and scheduling
summary: A container is a process with namespaced views and cgroup limits. Build from namespaces, images and cgroup v2 cpu.max and memory.max up to Kubernetes scheduling, probes, services, autoscaling and GPUs.
outcomes: Explain why a container is an ordinary process with namespaced views and cgroup limits, not a virtual machine
Compute the CPU a cgroup gets from cpu.max and predict the throttling stall per period
Explain why layer order decides build cache hits and why a deleted file still ships in the image
Predict whether a pod fits a node from its requests, and name its QoS class
Set probe budgets that exceed real startup time, and read an HPA or GPU scheduling decision

lessons.title: A container is a process with a narrowed view

blocks.md:
You run one command and a web server appears, apparently sealed off from everything else on the machine. It is tempting to picture a small virtual machine: its own kernel, its own CPUs, its own memory. That picture is wrong, and most production surprises in this course come from it being wrong.

A virtual machine runs a second operating system kernel on virtualized hardware. A container does not. A container is an ordinary Linux process, or a small tree of them, started by the same kernel that runs everything else on the node. Two kernel features make it feel separate: **namespaces**, which narrow what the process can see, and **cgroups**, which cap how much it may use.

Start with the naive attempt. `chroot` changes a process's idea of `/`, so it cannot name files outside a subtree. That is one view out of many. The process still sees every other process in `ps`, still shares the host network stack and its port numbers, and still runs as the host's user IDs. Changing one view is not isolation.

Linux generalizes the idea. The namespaces(7) manual page puts it precisely: a namespace wraps a global system resource in an abstraction that makes it appear to the processes within the namespace that they have their own isolated instance of that resource. Changes are visible inside and invisible outside. The page then says plainly that one use of namespaces is to implement containers.

There are eight namespace types, each created with its own `CLONE_NEW...` flag:

- **pid**: process IDs, so the container has its own pid 1 and its own numbering.
- **mount**: the mount table, so it has its own root filesystem.
- **net**: network devices, stacks and ports, so two containers can both bind port 80.
- **user**: user and group IDs, so root inside can map to an unprivileged ID outside.
- **ipc**: System V IPC and POSIX message queues.
- **uts**: hostname and NIS domain name.
- **cgroup**: the cgroup root directory the process sees.
- **time**: the boot and monotonic clocks.

`clone(2)` and `unshare(2)` create them, `setns(2)` joins an existing one. Creating most of them needs the `CAP_SYS_ADMIN` capability; user namespaces are the exception and have needed no privilege since Linux 3.8.

scenes.caption: Two containers are two ordinary processes. Nothing here is a second operating system: there is no guest kernel and no virtual hardware.
Namespaces narrow each process's view. Each has its own pid numbering, its own mount table, its own network stack and its own user IDs, so each can think it owns the machine.
cgroups cap how much each may consume. The limits are files in a directory, and they are enforced by the same kernel that runs everything else.

Both processes are scheduled by one kernel, which also serves their page faults and their TCP connections. That is why containers start in milliseconds, and why a node's kernel is shared fate for everything on it.

blocks.md: There is no container object in the kernel to point at. What exists is a `/proc/PID/ns/` directory per process, holding one symbolic link per namespace. The link text is the type plus an inode number, for example `uts:[4026531838]`. Two processes are in the same namespace exactly when those links resolve to the same inode, which a program can test with `stat(2)`. A container, from the kernel's side, is just a set of processes whose namespace links happen to match.

blocks.code:
# the kernel exposes namespaces as links, not as containers
readlink /proc/self/ns/pid
# pid:[4026531836]
readlink /proc/self/ns/net
# net:[4026531969]

# run a shell in fresh pid and mount namespaces (needs privilege)
unshare --pid --mount --fork --mount-proc /bin/sh

# inside that shell, the same binaries see a different world:
ps -e          # only this namespace's processes
readlink /proc/self/ns/pid   # a different inode number
blocks.caption: Nothing was installed and no image was used. unshare(2) plus a fork is already most of what a container runtime does for isolation.

blocks.md:
The pid namespace has one rule worth memorizing. The first process created in it gets pid 1 and becomes the namespace's init process. It inherits orphans, and other members of the namespace can only send it signals for which it has installed a handler, even if they are privileged. An ancestor namespace can force SIGKILL and SIGSTOP through, which is how the host still shuts a container down.

If that pid 1 terminates, the kernel sends SIGKILL to every remaining process in the namespace, and later attempts to fork into it fail with ENOMEM. This is why a container stops when its main process exits, and why an application running as pid 1 that ignores SIGTERM cannot be asked to shut down politely.

blocks.title: The same processes, two pid numberings

scenes.caption: From the host pid namespace, ps shows every process on the node: five here, including three that belong to container A.
From inside container A, the pid namespace renumbers what it can see and hides the rest. Host 4821 is pid 1 here; 4820 and 5107 do not exist at all.
If pid 1 of the namespace exits, the kernel sends SIGKILL to every remaining process in it. That is why a container dies when its main process dies, not because a supervisor noticed.

blocks.md: A container is not a virtual machine. Every container on a node runs on one kernel: the same scheduler, the same page cache, the same TCP stack, the same kernel bugs. By default `/proc/cpuinfo` and `/proc/meminfo` inside a container still report the host's hardware, because nothing in the namespace list virtualizes them. Code that sizes a thread pool from the CPU count it reads there will be badly wrong once a cgroup limit is applied, as the next lessons show.

blocks.prompt: Two containers on the same node both run a server bound to port 80, and neither uses host networking. A network stack has only one port 80. How can both succeed?
blocks.reveal:
Each container has its own **network namespace**, and a network namespace has its own network devices, its own routing table and its own port space. There are two independent port 80s, and neither process had to be changed.

What they cannot both have is port 80 in the host's own namespace. That is why publishing a port maps a host port into one container's namespace rather than letting both share a socket, and why two pods using host networking do collide.

blocks.question: A process inside a pid namespace runs the equivalent of kill -TERM 1, aiming at its own init process, which has installed no SIGTERM handler. What happens?
options: The signal is delivered, pid 1 exits, and the kernel SIGKILLs the rest of the namespace
Nothing reaches pid 1: a namespace member may only signal its init process for signals that init handles
The signal is redirected to the host's pid 1
The kernel rejects the call because pid 1 is in another namespace
blocks.explain: pid_namespaces(7) says only signals for which the init process has established a handler can be sent to it by other members of the namespace, and that this holds even for privileged processes. It exists to stop a container accidentally killing its own init. SIGKILL and SIGSTOP are forced through only when sent from an ancestor namespace.

blocks.question: Which statement about a container and a virtual machine running on the same node is correct?
options: Both run their own kernel, so a kernel panic affects only one of them
The container has its own scheduler, so cgroup limits are advisory
The container's threads are scheduled by the host kernel, which also serves their page faults and TCP connections
A container cannot share a CPU with other work
blocks.explain: The container's threads are plain tasks on the host kernel's run queues. That is what makes containers start in milliseconds, and also what makes the node's kernel shared fate for everything on it. A virtual machine does run a second kernel, at the cost of booting one.

lessons.title: What an image actually is: layers, unions and digests

blocks.md:
A container needs a root filesystem, and that is what an image provides. It is not a disk image and not a snapshot of a running machine. The OCI image specification defines it as a small set of content-addressed blobs.

Three kinds of object. A **manifest** lists the image's parts. A **config** holds the process settings (entrypoint, environment, working directory) and the ordered list of filesystem layers. The **layers** are the filesystem content. Every reference between them is a *descriptor*: a media type, a size in bytes, and a digest.

A layer is not a filesystem; it is a tar archive describing a **changeset**. Additions and modifications appear as ordinary tar entries. A removal cannot, because a tar has no way to say "this file is gone", so the spec defines a **whiteout**: an empty file named `.wh.` followed by the basename of the path to delete. Applying a layer extracts its tar, except that a whiteout hides the matching name in the layers below and then hides itself.

Whiteouts apply only to lower layers. A path deleted in layer 3 therefore still exists, in full, inside the blob for layer 1.

Stacking is the job of a union filesystem. On Linux that is usually overlayfs, which merges the directories named by `lowerdir` with one writable `upperdir` into a single `merged` tree. Lookup checks the upper layer first, then each lower in order, so the topmost definition of a path wins.

All of the container's writes land in the upper layer. Modifying a file that lives in a lower layer first copies it up, which the kernel documentation calls `copy_up`; deleting one writes a whiteout rather than touching the lower blob. That is why ten containers started from one image share a single on-disk copy of the read-only layers and differ only by a thin writable layer each.

blocks.title: overlayfs: stacking read-only layers under one writable layer

nodes.label: merged view: container 1 sees one tree

scenes.caption: The image's layers are mounted as lowerdirs, newest first, with one empty writable upperdir on top. Lookup searches the upper layer, then each lower in order, and the first definition of a path wins.
Reading /usr/bin/server: it is absent from the upper layer and from L3, and found in L2. No copy is made, and ten containers from this image read the same blob on disk.
Writing to that file cannot touch a read-only lower layer, so overlayfs first copies it up into the writable upper layer. Later reads then stop at the upper copy.
Deleting a file from a lower layer writes a whiteout marker into the upper layer. The name disappears from the merged view, and the bytes stay in the lower blob, untouched.
A second container from the same image adds only its own thin upperdir. The read-only layers are shared, which is why starting the tenth replica costs almost no disk.

blocks.md: Every blob is named by a **digest**: an algorithm plus an encoded hash of the exact bytes, such as `sha256:6c3c624b58db...`. The spec calls this content addressability, and two consequences follow immediately. A registry stores one copy of a blob however many images reference it, and a pull can skip any layer whose digest is already on the node. A client that trusts a digest can fetch the bytes from anywhere, hash them itself, and know it got the right content.

Two different hashes appear here and they are easy to confuse. The manifest's layer digest is taken over the blob as distributed, usually gzip or zstd compressed. The config's `rootfs.diff_ids` are **DiffIDs**: digests over each layer's *uncompressed* tar, in order from first to last. Compression output is not reproducible across tools, so the uncompressed tar is the stable identity of a changeset.

Identity of a *stack* needs more, because applying the same changesets in a different order gives a different filesystem. The spec folds the list into a **ChainID**:

blocks.caption: Digest here is the same hash function used for descriptors, and the separator is a single space. Because the previous ChainID is an input, the result depends on order.

blocks.code:
# toy example: two one-line "layers", hashed the way the spec hashes blobs
printf 'layer A: /usr/lib\n'    | shasum -a 256
# a053629867adb5eb38d...   = DiffID(A)
printf 'layer B: /app/server\n' | shasum -a 256
# 399fad200d70cc0cb56...   = DiffID(B)

# fold them: Digest(ChainID(previous) + " " + DiffID(next)),
# where each digest is the whole string, sha256: prefix included
# ChainID(A|B) = sha256:d1234bd967fa4cbb06a...
# ChainID(B|A) = sha256:29d0c5e04e145f80dcf...
blocks.caption: Computed with sha256 over exactly those bytes. Swapping the order gives an unrelated ChainID, which is why a stack's identity cannot be a hash of an unordered set of layers.

blocks.md:
Now the practical payoff. Each instruction in a container build produces a layer, and layers are a stack. The [build cache documentation](https://docs.docker.com/build/cache/) states the rule: once a layer changes, every layer after it must be rebuilt, even if it would produce identical bytes. The **order** of instructions, not just their content, decides what an edit costs.

So put the instructions that rarely change first and the ones that change on every commit last: dependency manifest, then dependency install, then source code, then build.

blocks.prompt: Two builds install the same dependencies and compile the same program. One copies the whole source tree and then installs dependencies; the other copies only the dependency manifest, installs, then copies the source. You edit one source file. What does each rebuild cost?
blocks.reveal:
Using 1 s per copy, 95 s to install and 40 s to compile:

- source first: the COPY layer changes, so install and compile both rerun. 1 + 95 + 40 = **136 s**.
- source last: the manifest is unchanged, so the install layer is a cache hit. 1 + 40 = **41 s**, about 3.3 times faster.

The push shrinks too. With layer sizes of 120 MB for dependencies, 2 MB for source and 45 MB for build output, the first order produces 167 MB of new blobs and the second 47 MB.

blocks.title: Layer order decides what an edit costs

scenes.caption: A cold build does the same work either way: copy, install dependencies, compile. Modelled at 1 s per copy, 95 s to install and 40 s to compile.
Now edit one source file. In the first order the COPY layer changes, and every layer after it must rerun even though it would build identical bytes: 1 + 95 + 40 = 136 s.
Same edit, second order. The dependency manifest did not change, so its install layer is a cache hit and only the late COPY and the compile rerun: 1 + 40 = 41 s, about 3.3 times faster.
Edit the dependency manifest instead and both orders pay the full install. Ordering does not make dependency changes cheap; it makes the common case, a source edit, cheap.

blocks.md: An image is an ordered list of content-addressed changesets plus a config. Everything else follows from that one sentence: identical layers are stored and transferred once, a deletion only adds a marker, and changing any layer invalidates every layer after it. Order your build steps from least to most frequently changing.

blocks.question: The last instruction in a build deletes a 300 MB cache directory that an earlier instruction created. What happens to the size of the pushed image?
options: It shrinks by 300 MB, because the final filesystem no longer contains the directory
The build fails, because whiteouts may not refer to lower layers
The earlier layer is rewritten without the directory
A new layer of whiteouts is added; the 300 MB stays in the earlier blob and is still pulled
blocks.explain: A removal is recorded as a whiteout in the new layer, and whiteouts only hide names in lower layers. The earlier blob is immutable and content addressed, so it still holds the bytes and is still downloaded. To avoid shipping them, create and delete within one layer, or build in one stage and copy only the output into a second.

blocks.question: Why does the image config record DiffIDs over uncompressed tars instead of reusing the manifest's layer digests?
options: Compression is not byte-for-byte reproducible across tools, so the uncompressed tar is the stable identity of a changeset
Hashing uncompressed data is cheaper
The manifest digests are not cryptographic hashes
Registries refuse to store compressed blobs
blocks.explain: The spec asks that layers be packed and unpacked reproducibly so the DiffID does not change, and warns explicitly not to confuse DiffIDs with the manifest's layer digests, which cover the distributed bytes. Hashing the uncompressed tar lets two tools agree that a layer is the same changeset even when their gzip output differs.

lessons.title: cgroup v2: cpu.max throttling and memory.max kills

blocks.md:
Namespaces answer what a process can see. They say nothing about how much it may use: a process alone in its own namespaces can still take every core and all the memory on the node. That is what control groups are for.

cgroups(7) describes them as a kernel feature that organizes processes into hierarchical groups whose use of resources can be limited and monitored, exposed through a pseudo-filesystem. Version 2, official since Linux 4.5, replaces version 1's one hierarchy per controller with a single unified hierarchy, usually mounted at `/sys/fs/cgroup`. A cgroup is a directory, its limits are files in that directory, and putting a process into it means writing a pid to `cgroup.procs`.

blocks.code:
# a cgroup is a directory; its limits are files
mkdir /sys/fs/cgroup/demo

# a controller only works in a child once the parent hands it down
echo '+cpu +memory' > /sys/fs/cgroup/cgroup.subtree_control

# half a CPU: 50000 microseconds of runtime per 100000 microsecond period
echo '50000 100000' > /sys/fs/cgroup/demo/cpu.max

# 512 MiB hard memory limit, in bytes
echo 536870912 > /sys/fs/cgroup/demo/memory.max

# move a process (and all its threads) in
echo 4821 > /sys/fs/cgroup/demo/cgroup.procs

# and read back what the limit cost you
cat /sys/fs/cgroup/demo/cpu.stat
cat /sys/fs/cgroup/demo/memory.events
blocks.caption: This is all a container runtime does for limits. An OCI runtime config expresses the same thing as cpu quota and period and memory limit fields, plus a unified map for writing cgroup v2 files directly.

blocks.md: `cpu.max` is a two-value file: a maximum amount of runtime and a period, both in microseconds. The default is `max 100000`, meaning no limit with a 100 ms period. Writing `50000 100000` says this group may consume up to 50 ms of CPU time in each 100 ms window. The ceiling expressed in CPUs is simply the ratio.

blocks.caption: A quota larger than the period means more than one CPU: 200000 over 100000 is 2 CPUs. Kubernetes writes the same number as 500m, where 1 CPU is one core or vCPU and the finest step allowed is 1m.

blocks.md:
The limit is not a rate shaper that slows each thread down. It is a budget per period. The group's runnable threads run at full hardware speed until this period's budget is gone, then the kernel stops all of them until the next period begins.

That makes the thread count matter in a way that surprises people. Four runnable threads under a 50 ms budget burn it in 50 / 4 = 12.5 ms of wall time and then sit throttled for 87.5 ms. Throughput is unchanged, 50 CPU-ms per period either way. What changes is the shape: more threads, shorter burst, longer stall, and any request that arrives during the stall waits for it.

blocks.title: cpu.max is a budget per period, not a speed limit

scenes.caption: cpu.max of 50000 100000: 50 ms of CPU time per 100 ms period. Four busy threads run at full speed and burn the whole budget in 50 / 4 = 12.5 ms, then all four are stopped for the remaining 87.5 ms.
The next period refills the budget and the pattern repeats. Over 1 s that is 10 periods, 10 of them throttled, and 875000 microseconds of throttled time in cpu.stat.

Same limit, one thread instead of four. Identical throughput, 50 CPU-ms per period, but the work is spread over 50 ms and the stall is 50 ms. Thread count changes the shape of the stall, never the ceiling.
Raise cpu.max to 200000 100000, which is 2 CPUs. The same four threads now get 50 ms of wall time each period before being throttled: more budget, so a longer burst and a shorter stall.

blocks.title: Threads do not buy throughput under a quota

scenes.caption: Milliseconds spent throttled in each 100 ms period, at a fixed cpu.max of 50000 100000. More runnable threads means the budget is spent sooner and the stall is longer: 50, 75, 87.5, 93.75.
CPU milliseconds actually delivered per period: identical in all four cases. The quota caps work, not parallelism. Threads only decide how tightly that work is bunched at the start of each period.

blocks.md:
You can measure this instead of guessing. `cpu.stat` in the cgroup reports `nr_periods`, `nr_throttled` and `throttled_usec`. For the four-thread example over one second that is 10 periods, 10 of them throttled, and 875000 microseconds throttled. A high ratio of `nr_throttled` to `nr_periods` on a service whose CPU graph looks calm is the signature of this bug.

`cpu.max` is a ceiling. The other CPU knob is `cpu.weight`, default 100, which decides how spare CPU is divided between sibling cgroups when the machine is busy. A cgroup with no `cpu.max` and a low weight is not capped at all; it simply loses when there is contention.

Nothing in `cpu.max` changes what the process sees. `/proc/cpuinfo` still lists every core on the node and `nproc` still counts them, so runtimes that size thread pools, garbage collector threads or worker counts from that number create far more runnable threads than the quota can feed. The result is exactly the figure above: a short burst, a long stall, and tail latency nobody can explain from a CPU utilization graph. Size pools from the quota, not from the hardware.

Memory behaves differently, because memory is not compressible: you cannot hand a process less memory per second the way you hand it less CPU per second.

`memory.max` is the hard limit, default `max`. When a cgroup's usage reaches it, the kernel first tries to reclaim pages from that cgroup. If reclaim cannot bring usage down, the out of memory (OOM) killer is invoked **inside the cgroup**, and `memory.events` counts `max` and then `oom_kill`. There are softer knobs: `memory.high` throttles the cgroup's processes and puts them under heavy reclaim pressure but never invokes the OOM killer, while `memory.min` and `memory.low` protect memory from reclaim instead of limiting it.

blocks.prompt: A cgroup has cpu.max of 50000 100000 and memory.max of 512 MiB. Its process tries to do four CPUs worth of work, and to allocate 600 MiB. What happens in each case?
blocks.reveal:
**CPU**: nothing is killed. The work is throttled and simply takes longer. Four threads get 50 ms of CPU per 100 ms period, so the job proceeds at one eighth of the rate four unlimited cores would give.

**Memory**: the kernel reclaims what it can, and when it cannot get under 512 MiB the cgroup's OOM killer terminates a process in it. Exceeding a CPU limit costs latency; exceeding a memory limit costs the process. Note the timing as well: the kill happens when an allocation presses against the limit, not when the limit is set, so a slow leak can run for hours before anything happens.

blocks.question: A service has cpu.max of 100000 100000 (1 CPU) and runs 8 busy threads. cpu.stat shows nr_periods 600 and nr_throttled 598. The service must answer within 50 ms. What is the right first move?
options: Add replicas and leave the limit alone, since one CPU is one CPU
Set the period and quota to 1000000 each, keeping 1 CPU but throttling less often
Reduce the thread count toward the quota, and raise the quota if the work genuinely needs more CPU
Remove memory.max so the kernel stops reclaiming
blocks.explain: With 8 threads and a 1 CPU budget the group burns its 100 ms of runtime in about 12.5 ms and stalls for 87.5 ms, which alone misses a 50 ms target. Fewer threads stretch the same budget across the period instead of bunching it at the start. Keeping 1 CPU with a 1 s period makes bursts and stalls ten times longer, not shorter, and memory limits have nothing to do with CPU throttling.

blocks.question: Which pairing correctly matches a cgroup v2 limit to what happens when a workload pushes past it?
options: cpu.max kills the process; memory.max throttles it
cpu.max stalls the threads until the next period; memory.max reclaims first, then OOM kills inside the cgroup
Both throttle: allocations are slowed to the configured rate
Both kill: the OOM killer handles CPU overuse as well
blocks.explain: CPU is compressible, so the kernel can withhold it and let the workload continue more slowly. Memory is not: once reclaim fails there is nothing left to withhold, so the cgroup's OOM killer runs and memory.events records the oom_kill. memory.high is the one memory knob that throttles rather than killing.

lessons.title: Kubernetes: pods, requests versus limits, and placement

blocks.md:
Everything so far happened on one machine. Kubernetes is the layer that decides which machine, and keeps that decision true as machines and processes fail.

Its unit is not a container but a [**pod**](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/): one or more containers that are always co-located and co-scheduled and run in a shared context. The documentation is explicit that this shared context is a set of Linux namespaces and cgroups, the same things that isolate a single container. Every container in a pod shares the network namespace, so they share one IP address and one port space and reach each other over `localhost`. Containers in different pods cannot, and must use the network.

You rarely create pods directly. A [**Deployment**](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/controllers/deployment/) declares a pod template and a replica count. The Deployment controller creates a **ReplicaSet**, and the ReplicaSet keeps exactly that many matching pods alive. Changing the template creates a *new* ReplicaSet and scales it up while scaling the old one down, which is what a rolling update is.

Two fields bound the churn: `maxUnavailable` and `maxSurge`, both 25% by default. During a rollout the number of pods stays between replicas minus maxUnavailable and replicas plus maxSurge.

blocks.title: Deployment, ReplicaSet and a rolling update

scenes.caption: A Deployment holds a pod template and a replica count. It creates a ReplicaSet, and the ReplicaSet is what keeps exactly four matching pods alive, recreating any that die.
Change the template and the Deployment creates a second ReplicaSet rather than editing pods in place. maxSurge of 25% of 4 allows one extra pod, so a fifth may exist while the rollout runs.
Once a new pod is Ready, an old one can go. maxUnavailable of 25% of 4 means at least three must stay available at every moment, which is what keeps a rollout from becoming an outage.
The old ReplicaSet ends at zero pods but is kept, which is what a rollback scales back up. The Deployment itself never touched a pod: it only resized two ReplicaSets.

blocks.md:
Each container may state two numbers per resource, and they do completely different jobs.

A **request** is what the scheduler uses. It picks a node with enough unclaimed capacity, and the **kubelet**, the Kubernetes agent that runs on every node and starts its containers, reserves at least that much for the container. A **limit** is the cap the kernel enforces, and here the first half of this course reappears: the kubelet turns a CPU limit into the cgroup's `cpu.max` and a memory limit into `memory.max`. So a CPU limit is enforced by throttling, and a memory limit by an OOM kill when the kernel detects pressure, exactly as in the previous lesson.

A container may use more than its request when the node has spare capacity. It may never exceed its limit. If you set a limit and no request, Kubernetes copies the limit into the request.

The capacity the scheduler divides up is not the machine's capacity. The kubelet [reserves resources](https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/administer-cluster/reserve-compute-resources/) for itself and the container runtime (`kube-reserved`), for system daemons (`system-reserved`), and holds back an eviction threshold. What is left is **allocatable**, and the documentation states that the scheduler does not over-subscribe it.

blocks.caption: On a 4 core, 16 GiB node with kube-reserved 100m and 1Gi, system-reserved 100m and 512Mi, and a 256Mi eviction threshold: allocatable is 3800m CPU and 14592Mi memory, not 4000m and 16384Mi. The figures below use those numbers.

blocks.md: Placement itself is [two steps](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/scheduling-eviction/kube-scheduler/). **Filtering** keeps only the *feasible* nodes, for example those whose unclaimed allocatable still covers every one of the pod's requests. **Scoring** ranks the survivors, the highest score wins, and equal scores are broken at random. The result is written to the API server, which the documentation calls binding. If no node is feasible the pod stays Pending: nothing is ever squeezed onto an overfull node.

blocks.title: Filtering: a pod fits only if every request fits

scenes.caption: Each node has 3800m and 14592Mi allocatable. Subtracting the requests of the pods already placed there leaves the free amounts shown. pod-1 requests 1000m and 6144Mi.
CPU filter: node-b has 800m free, less than the 1000m requested, so it is not feasible. Its 11992Mi of free memory does not help at all.
Memory filter: node-c has 2092Mi free against a 6144Mi request, so it drops out too. A node can be short on one dimension and useless despite plenty of the other.
Only node-a survives filtering, so scoring has a single candidate and the scheduler binds pod-1 there. Had no node survived, the pod would simply stay Pending.
pod-2 arrives wanting 700m and 2048Mi. node-a now has only 500m and 1448Mi left and fails, while node-b and node-c both fit, so this time scoring has a real choice and ties are broken at random.

blocks.md:
Requests and limits also decide a pod's **QoS class**, which decides who dies first when a node runs short.

- **Guaranteed**: every container sets CPU and memory requests and limits, all nonzero, with request equal to limit for both resources.
- **Burstable**: not Guaranteed, but at least one container sets some CPU or memory request or limit.
- **BestEffort**: no container sets any CPU or memory request or limit at all.

Under node resource pressure the kubelet evicts BestEffort pods first, then Burstable, then Guaranteed; and when the eviction is caused by resource pressure, only pods using more than their requests are candidates. A pod with no requests is therefore both invisible to the scheduler's arithmetic and first in the queue to be evicted.

The sum of **limits** on a node may exceed allocatable: a limit is a per-container ceiling, and overcommitting ceilings is normal. The sum of **requests** may not, because requests are what the scheduler subtracts. Two mistakes follow. Setting limits only copies each limit into the request, so the node looks full long before it is. Setting requests only leaves no ceiling, so one pod can take everything spare and push the node into eviction.

blocks.question: Nodes have 3800m allocatable CPU and 14592Mi allocatable memory. Free right now: node-a 1500m and 7592Mi, node-b 800m and 11992Mi, node-c 2000m and 2092Mi. A pod requests 1000m and 6144Mi. Which nodes are feasible?
options: node-a and node-c, because both have enough CPU
All three, because no limits were set
node-b and node-c, because each has the most of one resource
node-a only
blocks.explain: Filtering needs every requested resource to fit at the same time. node-b fails on CPU (800 < 1000) and node-c fails on memory (2092 < 6144), so only node-a clears both and scoring has one candidate. Having plenty of one resource does not help when the other is short, which is how a cluster ends up with idle CPU and nowhere to put a pod.

blocks.question: A pod has one container with requests of cpu 200m and memory 256Mi, and limits of cpu 1 and memory 256Mi. What is its QoS class?
options: Guaranteed, because the memory request equals the memory limit
BestEffort, because the CPU is not pinned
Burstable, because the CPU request and limit differ
Guaranteed, because both requests are set
blocks.explain: Guaranteed requires request to equal limit for both CPU and memory, in every container. Memory matches here but CPU does not (200m against 1000m), so the pod is Burstable: evicted after BestEffort pods and before Guaranteed ones, and only while it is using more than its requests.

lessons.title: Probes, Services and DNS: liveness is not readiness

blocks.md:
A scheduled pod is not a working pod. Kubernetes needs two separate answers about a container, and conflating them causes some of the most expensive incidents in this field.

The kubelet runs three kinds of probe.

- A **liveness** probe that fails more times than its tolerance makes the kubelet restart the container.
- A **readiness** probe that fails makes the EndpointSlice controller remove the pod's IP address from the EndpointSlices of every Service that matches it. The container keeps running and keeps being probed, so it can come back. A **Service** is the stable name in front of a set of pods and an **EndpointSlice** is its list of pod addresses; both are built up later in this lesson.
- A **startup** probe runs only at startup. Until it succeeds, liveness and readiness probes do not run at all. If it fails its threshold, the container is killed and restarted.

All three share the same timing fields, and the defaults are where the trouble starts:

- `initialDelaySeconds`: default 0, minimum 0.
- `periodSeconds`: default 10, minimum 1.
- `timeoutSeconds`: default 1, minimum 1.
- `successThreshold`: default 1, and must be 1 for liveness and startup probes.
- `failureThreshold`: default 3, minimum 1.

So a liveness probe tolerates roughly initialDelaySeconds plus failureThreshold x periodSeconds before it restarts the container. The documentation names that quantity directly: if your container usually takes longer than that to start, you need a startup probe.

blocks.title: Probe budgets against a 40 second startup

scenes.caption: The app needs 40 s to warm up. Its only probe is liveness with initialDelaySeconds 10, periodSeconds 5 and failureThreshold 3, so the budget is 10 + 3 x 5 = 25 s. Probes at 10, 15 and 20 s all fail.

So the container is killed at 20 s and starts over, and the clock restarts with it. It never reaches second 40. This is the CrashLoopBackOff whose logs show nothing wrong with the application. Simplified: each later restart is also delayed a little longer.

Add a startup probe on the same endpoint with periodSeconds 10 and failureThreshold 30, a budget of 300 s. It fails at 0, 10, 20 and 30 s and succeeds at 40. While it has not succeeded, liveness and readiness do not run at all.

Only now do the other two begin, and their delays start from the startup success. Readiness (initialDelay 0, period 5) probes at 40, 45, 50, 55; liveness (initialDelay 10, period 5) first probes at 50. Traffic starts at 40 s instead of never.

blocks.code:
startupProbe:
  httpGet: { path: /healthz, port: 8080 }
  periodSeconds: 10
  failureThreshold: 30    # 30 x 10 = 300 s allowed to start
livenessProbe:
  httpGet: { path: /healthz, port: 8080 }
  initialDelaySeconds: 10
  periodSeconds: 5
  failureThreshold: 3     # tolerates 10 + 3 x 5 = 25 s of unhealth
readinessProbe:
  httpGet: { path: /ready, port: 8080 }
  periodSeconds: 5        # /ready may check dependencies; /healthz must not
blocks.caption: Startup and liveness deliberately share an endpoint, as the docs suggest, so the slow-start case and the wedged case are judged by the same check with different budgets.

blocks.md:
Three probe mistakes, worst first.

1. A **liveness** probe that checks a dependency: the database hiccups, every replica fails liveness, and the kubelet restarts the whole fleet with cold caches.
2. A **readiness** probe on a shared dependency: every replica goes NotReady at once, so the Service has no backends, which is worse than degraded.
3. **No startup probe** on a slow starter: the container never finishes initializing, and the only symptom is a restart count.

Pod IP addresses are not stable; a rolling update replaces every one of them. A [**Service**](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/services-networking/service/) is the stable name in front of them. The default type, `ClusterIP`, gets a virtual cluster IP, and its `selector` tells a controller which pods belong to it. That controller continuously keeps the Service's **EndpointSlices** in step as pods appear, become ready and disappear.

This is the exact seam where readiness matters: readiness does not slow a pod down or restart it, it removes the pod's address from the EndpointSlices so new connections stop arriving.

Names come from [cluster DNS](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/services-networking/dns-pod-service/). A normal Service gets an A or AAAA record at `my-svc.my-namespace.svc.cluster-domain.example` resolving to its cluster IP. A **headless** Service, one with no cluster IP, gets records at the same kind of name that resolve to the set of IPs of all the pods it selects, which is how clients that must address individual replicas (shards, a stateful database) find them. Named ports additionally get SRV records of the form `_port-name._port-protocol.my-svc.my-namespace.svc.cluster-domain.example`.

Inside a pod the resolver's search list makes short forms work: `my-svc` from the same namespace, `my-svc.my-namespace` from another.

blocks.title: From a DNS name to a ready pod, and back out again

scenes.caption: Discovery is DNS. A normal Service has an A record at my-svc.my-namespace.svc.cluster-domain.example that resolves to its stable cluster IP, not to any pod.
The client connects to that virtual IP. The node's proxy rewrites the connection to one pod IP and port drawn from the Service's EndpointSlices, which list only the endpoints currently Ready.
Backend A's readiness probe starts failing. The EndpointSlice controller removes its IP from every Service that selects it. Nothing kills the container: it keeps running and keeps being probed.
New connections now reach only pods still in the slices. Backend A is skipped while it recovers, and rejoins the moment readiness passes again. A liveness failure would instead have restarted it.

blocks.question: An application takes 40 s to warm its caches. Its only probe is a liveness probe with initialDelaySeconds 10, periodSeconds 5 and failureThreshold 3. What do you observe?
options: The pod becomes Ready at 40 s, because liveness failures only affect traffic
The container is restarted at about 20 s and keeps restarting, because the budget is 10 + 3 x 5 = 25 s
The pod stays Pending until the probe succeeds
Nothing: the kubelet waits for a first success before it starts counting failures
blocks.explain: Probes at 10, 15 and 20 seconds all fail, which reaches failureThreshold, so the kubelet restarts the container and the clock starts over. The fix is a startup probe on the same endpoint: periodSeconds 10 with failureThreshold 30 allows 300 s, succeeds at 40 s, and only then lets liveness and readiness begin.

blocks.question: Every replica of a service uses one endpoint for both liveness and readiness, and that endpoint returns 503 while the database is unreachable. The database restarts for 90 seconds. What happens?
options: Only readiness is affected, so traffic pauses and then resumes
The Service keeps routing, because liveness does not touch EndpointSlices
The scheduler moves the pods to other nodes
Every replica fails liveness and is restarted together, so recovery is delayed by cold starts on top of the database outage
blocks.explain: A liveness failure restarts the container; a readiness failure only removes it from the EndpointSlices. Because one shared endpoint drives both, a dependency outage triggers both everywhere at once: the fleet goes NotReady and is also restarted, so every replica returns cold. Liveness should test only the process; readiness is the right place to admit a dependency is down.

lessons.title: Autoscaling and GPU scheduling: two control loops

blocks.md:
A replica count is a guess. A **HorizontalPodAutoscaler** turns it into a control loop: read a metric, compare it to a target, write a new replica count through the workload's `scale` subresource, which is why the same object works for Deployments and StatefulSets.

The loop is not continuous. It runs on an interval set by the `--horizontal-pod-autoscaler-sync-period` flag on the controller manager, 15 seconds by default. Everything the autoscaler does is therefore quantized to that tick.
The core of the algorithm is a single ratio.

blocks.caption: Straight from the autoscaling documentation. For a CPU target given as a utilization percentage, the current value is each pod's usage expressed as a percentage of its CPU request, averaged across the pods.

blocks.md:
Work an example. Four replicas, each container requesting 500m CPU, with a target average utilization of 50%, which is 250m per pod. The pods are averaging 400m.

The ratio is 400 / 250 = 1.6, so the desired count is the ceiling of 4 x 1.6 = 6.4, which is 7. The controller skips scaling when the ratio is close enough to 1.0, within a tolerance of 0.1 by default, and 1.6 is far outside it.

Now check that 7 is stable. If total demand stays at 4 x 400 = 1600m, each of 7 pods averages 1600 / 7 = 228.57m, a ratio of 0.914. That is 0.086 away from 1.0, inside the tolerance, so the loop stops. Six replicas would have been stable too (ratio 1.067). The tolerance is exactly what stops the autoscaler hunting between them every 15 seconds.

blocks.title: Where the HPA's replica count comes from

scenes.caption: At 4 replicas with a 250m target, an average of 400m per pod gives a ratio of 1.6, and the ceiling of 4 x 1.6 = 6.4 is 7 replicas. The curve is a staircase because of that ceiling.
Recompute at 7 replicas. If total demand is unchanged, each pod now averages 1600 / 7 = 228.57m, a ratio of 0.914. That is 0.086 from 1.0, inside the default tolerance of 0.1, so the loop stops here.
Lower the target to 200m and the same measurement demands more replicas everywhere. The target, not the load, is what sets the fleet size, and halving it roughly doubles the bill.

blocks.md: Scaling down is deliberately slower than scaling up. The `behavior.scaleDown.stabilizationWindowSeconds` field, 300 by default, makes the controller look back over the desired counts it computed in the last five minutes and take the highest one. That is a rolling maximum, and its purpose is to stop the autoscaler deleting pods it will have to recreate moments later.

A CPU utilization target is a percentage of the CPU **request**, not of the node or the limit. If a container has no relevant request, the docs say pod CPU utilization is undefined and the autoscaler takes no action for that metric, so the HPA quietly does nothing.

Because the metric is per pod, the HPA can only fix a shortage of pods. If each pod is already throttled by its own `cpu.max`, adding replicas treats the symptom; raising the limit treats the cause.

GPUs reach pods through the [**device plugin**](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/extend-kubernetes/compute-storage-net/device-plugins/) framework, a second control loop with much stricter arithmetic. A vendor's plugin runs on the node, registers with the kubelet over a gRPC `Registration` service, names what it advertises using the `vendor-domain/resourcetype` scheme (`nvidia.com/gpu`, `amd.com/gpu`), and streams its list of healthy devices. The kubelet advertises that count in the node status, and the scheduler filters on it exactly as it filters on CPU and memory.

Three restrictions make GPUs behave unlike CPU, and all three matter:

- Extended resources are **integer only and cannot be overcommitted**. There is no 0.5 of a GPU and no oversubscription by default.
- Devices **cannot be shared between containers**.
- GPUs are specified in `limits`. You may omit `requests` (the limit is copied into it) or set them equal, but you cannot set a request without a limit.

blocks.title: GPUs are allocated whole, and not overcommitted

scenes.caption: The vendor's device plugin reported 8 healthy devices, so the kubelet advertises nvidia.com/gpu: 8 in the node status. The scheduler then filters on it like any other resource.
A training pod asks for 4 in limits. Because extended resources cannot be overcommitted, those 4 devices leave the schedulable pool for the pod's whole lifetime, whether the GPUs are busy or idle.
Two more pods take 2 and 1. Seven of eight are allocated, one is free, and no device is shared between containers.
A fourth pod requests 2 GPUs. Only 1 is free, requests are integer, and there is no fractional allocation, so the pod stays Pending until a device is released or another node has 2 free.

blocks.question: A Deployment runs 4 replicas, each container requesting 500m CPU. The HPA targets 50% average utilization and the pods average 400m. What does the controller write, and does it keep scaling?
options: 6 now, then 7 on the next tick
8, doubling because utilization is 80%
7, and it stops: at 7 replicas the ratio is 0.914, inside the default 0.1 tolerance
5, because the controller adds at most one replica per period
blocks.explain: The target per pod is 50% of the 500m request, so 250m. The ratio is 400 / 250 = 1.6 and the ceiling of 4 x 1.6 = 6.4 is 7. If total demand is unchanged, 7 pods average 1600 / 7 = 228.57m, a ratio of 0.914, which is 0.086 from 1.0 and inside the tolerance, so the loop settles. A later scale down would additionally wait out the 300 s stabilization window.

blocks.question: Two inference pods each need about half of one GPU's memory and compute. You want both on one GPU using plain nvidia.com/gpu requests. What does Kubernetes do?
options: It splits the device, because GPU requests may be fractional like CPU
Only one pod gets a device: extended resources are integer and not overcommittable, and devices are not shared between containers
It schedules both and lets the driver time-slice them
Both pods fail admission
blocks.explain: Device plugin resources are handed out as whole integer devices that cannot be overcommitted or shared between containers, so two pods asking for 1 need 2 devices and the second waits. Sharing one physical card requires a mechanism outside this resource model, which works by presenting the card as several devices that the plugin advertises separately, so Kubernetes still allocates whole units.

blocks.md: Four sentences for the whole course. A container is a process the host kernel schedules, with namespaced views of pids, mounts, network and users, and cgroup files capping what it may use. Its image is an ordered list of content-addressed changesets, so changing one invalidates every layer after it. Kubernetes places pods by **requests** and enforces **limits** by writing `cpu.max` and `memory.max`. Probes, autoscaling and device plugins are thin loops on top, each failing predictably.
